Photograph: Michael Varaklas/AP View image in fullscreen Firefighters battle a wildfire near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens, on Sunday. Photograph: Michael Varaklas/AP Greece Two helicopters collide outside Athens as Greece battles to control wildfires Fire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capital Helena Smith in Athens and agencies Sun 2 Aug 2026 13.36 EDT First published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens, killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified. Gale-force winds that have pushed flames towards settlements on Athens’ western fringes were caught on video on Sunday downing one of the helicopters. “The pilots ... were taken unconscious to hospital, where their death was confirmed,” said the fire department’s director of communications, Vassilis Vathrakogiannis. The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said the two dead were a Dane and a Greek. The two crew members of the second helicopter were rescued. As Europe’s wildfire crisis fractured along different routes, and in further proof of the destructive force of climate-driven wildfires across the continent, the blazes ripped through Greece’s tinder-dry landscape, up mountain slopes and down to the sea, before encroaching on the capital. Warning of “extremely difficult” days ahead, Mitsotakis underlined the threat posed by gusts that in recent days have exceeded 78mph (125km/h). “When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely,” he wrote on social media. More than 100 homes were destroyed overnight in fires that broke out around the popular coastal village of Porto Germeno, about 45 miles (70km) north-west of Athens. By Sunday, more than 500 firefighters and forest commandos had been dispatched to keep the flames at bay. View image in fullscreen A firefighting helicopter drops water over a forest near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens, on Sunday. Photograph: Michael Varaklas/AP The eastern Mediterranean, no stranger to wildfires, has had a relatively calm summer to date, leaving Greeks to watch in horror as the blazes have hit farther west. As the advance of wildfires in Spain was finally curbed and officials in France announced that a mega-fire – four times the size of Paris – had begun to be contained, the blazes in Greece have prompted mass evacuations and devastated huge swathes of land from Crete to the southern Peloponnese, the Ionian isle of Cephalonia and islands across the Aegean. Last week three Greek firefighters died from injuries sustained while they fought blazes. Extreme winds have been a blessing – in bringing down summer temperatures – but also a curse, with their-gale force strength obstructing firefighting efforts. Greece’s civil protection minister, Evangelos Tournas, a retired air force general, said at the weekend that the fire department had been “pushed to its limits”. He said high winds had created “extremely difficult conditions resulting in many cases where aircraft either cannot draw water or cannot carry out drops due to extreme turbulence”. View image in fullscreen People using olive branches to beat back the flames in the Megara valley, in western Attica, Greece, on Sunday. Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/Reuters France’s largest wildfire remained contained after 224,000 people were forced to flee in what may have been the largest peacetime evacuation in French history. But active pockets still burned across 160 sq miles (420 sq km) of devastated forest. Thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde mega-fire and a second blaze in Provence that had stopped advancing but remained uncontained. “The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said on Sunday, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped and whose perimeter has been contained. The region remained under France’s highest red forest fire alert. Dry conditions and soaring temperatures around Bordeaux, combined with afternoon winds, created a continued risk of renewed flames. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A deer in the forest in Le Temple, Gironde. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Additional firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected on Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation. Weather tracker: Why Europe’s wildfires are proving so fierce and difficult to stop Read more Hundreds of miles away, nearly 1,500 firefighters were battling a separate fire in the south-eastern Var department that tore through roughly 7 sq miles in little more than a day. Authorities said the fire in the Gros Bessillon hills was stabilised on Sunday morning, meaning its perimeter had not expanded overnight. But unlike the Gironde fire, it had not yet been declared contained. Firefighting aircraft supported crews working to keep the flames away from villages among the vineyards, olive groves and wooded hills of the region known as Green Provence. About 2,500 people were evacuated as the fire threatened communities. The blaze was the fourth major fire to strike the central Var since 19 July. A separate, smaller fire near Brignoles earlier in the week forced the Hollywood actor George Clooney and his family, along with about 700 other residents , to evacuate before it was brought under control. View image in fullscreen Smoke above Montfort-sur-Argens, near Correns, in Var, on Saturday. Photograph: Manon Cruz/Reuters The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said France’s wildfires were generally under control but cautioned that conditions remained highly changeable. He announced that a national coordinator attached to the prime minister’s office would oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. More than 450 sq miles have burned across France since the beginning of the year. Fires in France and Spain alone have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and holiday sites, emptied communities at the height of the summer and stretched firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous disasters. The crisis is unfolding on the world’s fastest-warming continent. Europe has heated at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Higher temperatures and prolonged drought leave forests and scrubland drier and more combustible, allowing fires to spread faster and burn more intensely. Human-caused climate breakdown doubled the likelihood of the extreme fire conditions that fuelled the French blazes, scientists at World Weather Attribution calculated in a rapid analysis on Thursday while the fires were still burning. https://languagehat.com/the-layering-of-.text: languagehat.com The Layering of East Slavic. A paper by Michael S. Flier ( Harvard Ukrainian Studies 35 1-4 [2017-2018]: 31-42) begins by quoting Roman Szporluk on the origins of Ukrainian ethnic and cultural identity and asks “If the imagined community began to emerge in the late eighteenth century, when did the Ukrainian vernacular begin to delimit itself vis-à-vis its neighbors?” Flier goes on to quote George Shevelov to the effect that “a continuum has existed from the earliest local changes within Common Slavic to the present,” then gets to the meat of his paper: It is one thing to worry about labels, but it is quite another to examine the typology of the linguistic systems on East Slavic territory and uncover the relationship among specific changes. The goal is to establish not simply a list of distinctive characteristics, as Shevelov would have it, but to reveal a hierarchy of change and therefore a more accurate evaluation of linguistic data.[ 6 ] Thus, we are not as interested in registering Change A and Change B as we are in the assertion that Change B implies Change A and if B is in place it is no longer possible to return to the status quo ante, that is pre-A. My intent here is to make use of advances in Slavic historical linguistics since the publication of Shevelov’s encyclopedic Ukrainian historical phonology three and a half decades ago, knowledge that sheds new light on the chronological layering of East Slavic and thus provides a relative time frame for marking such fundamental typological shifts. I will focus here on internally motivated sound change precisely because it is based on linguistic data least subject to conscious alteration on the part of speakers. We want to consider the language of speakers throughout Ukrainian territory, especially those at a far remove from the scriptoria and bureaucratic offices of urban elites. Members of this latter group are much more likely to be affected by the need for new abstract vocabulary or socially prestigious speech, desiderata that often lead to calques or direct borrowings, particularly from neighboring languages of power such as Polish or Russian. En passant we might note that both of these prestigious and influential languages have had a heavy steady stream of borrowing and calquing of their own. For now we will forget the self-reflective elites: we will be interested in when and how the non-elite speech communities of East Slavic began to diverge phonologically, never to proceed along the same trajectory again. The Late Common Slavic speech community that resulted from the great Slavic migrations of the sixth and seventh centuries yielded some major changes that permit us to distinguish typologically the Slavic south from the Slavic north, and within the latter, the Slavic east from the Slavic west. […] With the vast geographical expanse of East linguistic territory in mind, I’d like to focus attention on one particular isogloss (here, Isogloss 1), one dramatic linguistic boundary line, that bisects East Slavic territory laterally where modern Ukrainian dialects are juxtaposed to Russian, Belarusian, and Polish dialects (see fig. 1). Isogloss 1 looks like the marker of a fairly straightforward, simple difference in pronunciation. In the environment before the front vowel e from Late Common Slavic * e and strong front jer * ĭ (both hereafter symbolized by * e ), dialects north and west of Isogloss 1 permit only the reflexes of sharped (palatalized, soft) labial and dental consonants, e.g., R p’eči ‘stove’ (GEN-LOC-DAT-SG), z’el’en’i ‘green; greenery’ (GEN-LOC-DEN-SG), d’es’at’ ‘ten’, p’en’ ‘stump’ (пень/пня), d’en’ ‘day’ (день/дня); Br p’eči (печы), z’el’en’i (зелені), ʒ’es’ac’ (дзесяць), p’en’ (пень/пня), ʒ’en’ (дзень/дня). Polish shows analogous distribution, e.g., P p’ec ‘bake’ (piec, INFINITIVE), źeleńi (zieleni), ʒ´eśęć (dziesięć), p’eń (pień/pnia), ʒ´eń (dzień/dnia).[ 8 ] Dialects south and east of Isogloss 1 permit only the reflexes of hard (nonpalatalized, plain) labial and dental consonants in this environment, e.g., U peči, zelen’i, des’at’, pen’ (пень/пня), den’ (день/дня).[ 9 ] In early East and West Slavic, sharping was predictable and thus not phonemic for any consonants.[ 10 ] They were either inherently sharped (palatals) or plain (velars), or contextually sharped or plain (labials and dentals).[ 11 ] […] Sharped and plain variants of labials and dentals could not contrast with one another, and were thus not distinctive, not phonemic. But the apparently simple Isogloss1 turns out to be more complex than it appears, representing the effects not of a single change, but of a cluster of changes resulting from the last historical event shared by all the Slavic languages: the so-called jer shift. […] The presence of Isogloss1 would seem to indicate that at some point, dialects to the south simply reinterpreted sharped labials and dentals before e as plain, but exactly when has not been easy to determine. The orthographic evidence from East Slavic texts is moot, with sequences such as ПЕ, БЕ, МЕ, ТЕ, СЕ, НЕ indicating nothing about the presence or absence of sharping (печи, тебе, мене, село). Indeed, after examining all the traditional evidence concerning the presence or absence of subphonemic sharping in East Slavic, in particular on Ukrainian territory before the jer shift, Shevelov came to no conclusion, but ultimately leaned towards the idea that labials and dentals were not sharped before e from Late Common Slavic * e .[ 15 ] But contemporaneous work on the development of the vowels e and ê in East and West Slavic permits a reassessment of that position. Shevelov saw inexplicable inconsistency in the way that original sequences of CeCŭ rendered the consonant preceding e as sharped before a later i < e , but plain before a retained e , e.g., Rs selŭ ‘village’ (GEN-PL) > U s’il but Rs klenŭ ‘maple’ > U klen . In a comprehensive analysis of evidence of the e > o change in East and West Slavic and the ê > a change in West Slavic, Henning Andersen has provided strong support for the presence of subphonemic sharping of labials and dentals in the environment before front vowels before the jer shift.[ 16 ] […] Relevant here is the most startling hypothesis in Andersen’s study, namely, that the presence of pitch accent instead of stress accent during the jer shift in all but northern regions of Ukraine resulted in the shortening of all syllables except the pretonic, a Central Slavic feature that Ukrainian shared with Polish and Slovak.[ 19 ] […] These developments, occurring at the time of the jer shift in the twelfth century, meant that in all of Rus´, the opposition sharped/plain was neutralized as sharped in the environment before ê of any origin. In the environment before e , however, the sharped/plain opposition was neutralized as sharped in dialects north and west of Isogloss 1 and as plain in dialects south and east of Isogloss 1—that is, in proto-Ukrainian territory. This remarkable fact about Ukrainian distinguishes it from all of its neighbors, current and historical, that might have had any influence on the development of Ukrainian, namely, Russian, Belarusian, and Polish.[ 24 ] He goes into a great many details that I have omitted; interested parties will want to click through and examine the evidence, and I hope those with more understanding than I of this sort of thing will give an informed judgment on the plausibility of the idea. Me, I can’t help but notice the use (unfamiliar to me) of “sharp” to mean ‘palatalized’; I like it because it’s a lot shorter, but I wonder how widespread it is. It is not, for example, in the OED, which has only “ 8.c. Phonetics . ( a ) Used to express the acoustic quality of the high-front vowels; ( b ) a designation for unvoiced consonants. Obsolete in technical use.” And I thank my old MeFi pal clavdivs for sharing the link with me. Diphtongisation of long vowels 2. Diphtong > vowel + consonantal glide 3. Consonantal glides > /j:/, /v:/ 4. Affricatisation of c /j(:)/, /v(:)/ (palatal and rounded affricates, respectively) 5. Dissimilation of vowels before a palatal or rounded affricate. 6 Devoicing and depalatalisation/unrounding of affricates Probably because that’s where the perceived irregularities are, skerping is used in synchronic descriptions for the vowel outcomes of stage 5, while the diachronic process earned its name from the consonantal effects in stages 2-4 + 6. Romania-Bulgaria-Turkey trilateral / Photo: fb.com Ștefan Radu Oprea Roxana Vasile , 29.10.2026, 14:00 While the Defense Ministers of Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey were meeting in Sofia on Wednesday to discuss measures to protect civilian shipping, amidst reciprocal attacks between Russia and Ukraine, a new incident occurred in the Black Sea. A merchant vessel, which had departed from the Israeli port of Haifa and was bound for the Romanian port of Constanța, was struck by drones near the Bulgarian coast. This marks the fifth merchant ship to be attacked by drones off the Bulgarian coast of the Black Sea this month. Furthermore, since the beginning of the summer, no fewer than 11 merchant vessels have been struck or sunk near the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania. These incidents have resulted in casualties as well as massive material damage. While initially described as isolated events, the steadily rising number of such incidents has become a serious cause for alarm; maritime traffic is now in genuine danger due to drones, as well as due to Russian or Ukrainian naval mines drifting into the area. Yet, the Black Sea serves as a strategic hub connecting Europe, Central Asia, and the Middle East. Consequently, control over this basin and its stability are essential to the energy, commercial, and military security of the entire European continent. Following a meeting of the Supreme Council of National Defense (CSAT) in Bucharest, a North Atlantic Council session in Brussels, and discussions at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, all taking place last week, a meeting of the Defense Ministers of Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey was held in Sofia on Wednesday. According to a statement from the Romanian Ministry of National Defense, Radu Oprea, Dimitar Stoyanov, and Yaşar Güler discussed measures necessary to strengthen both Allied cooperation in the Black Sea and trilateral cooperation. These efforts are intended to help prevent escalation, protect human lives, and ensure the safe conduct of civilian activities in the Black Sea. Minister Oprea firmly condemned the attacks on commercial shipping, emphasizing that they represent a substantial escalation of the risks associated with the Russian Federation’s war of aggression against Ukraine. He highlighted the necessity of upholding freedom of navigation and protecting civilian vessels and maritime infrastructure. The Romanian official presented the direct implications of these developments for Romania’s security, as well as the importance of NATO support in strengthening capabilities for surveillance, early warning, and countering drones. At the same time, he emphasized the need to bolster protection measures for critical infrastructure and energy assets within Romania’s exclusive economic zone. Regarding the development of trilateral cooperation, it was agreed to improve maritime situation awareness, to intensify information exchange, and strengthen coordination among the naval forces of the three states. Furthermore, the importance of continuing cooperation within the framework of the trilateral initiative for countering sea mines, MCM Black Sea, was highlighted. “Because the security of the Black Sea is essential to the security of Romania, the region, and the entire North Atlantic Alliance,” stated Defense Minister Radu Oprea.
